questions.problem:
Find $\text{E}[4(X-1)],$ given that random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4},\, & 1\le x\le 2,\,1\le y\le {x}^{2}; \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)=4(x-1).
$$

Now, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,1\le y\le {x}^{2}\},$ where $f(x,y)$ is nonzero.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14215461/assets/bd8d2d36a0fe570e6ccdb096c6c39bc9c9edeed9b008dada504801025055438f.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[4(X-1)] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}4(x-1)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}4(x-1)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{{x}^{2}}4(x-1)\cdot \frac{3}{4}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{2}(x-1){\int }_{1}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{2}(x-1)[y]_{y=1}^{y={x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{2}(x-1)({x}^{2}-1)\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{2}({x}^{3}-{x}^{2}-x+1)\text{d}x \\  & =3{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x]}_{x=1}^{x=2} \\  & =3[(4-\frac{8}{3}-2+2)-(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+1)] \\  & =3(\frac{4}{3}-\frac{5}{12}) \\  & =\frac{11}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find $\text{E}[{(X+Y)}^{2}],$ given that random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4},\, & y\le x\le 4-y,\,0\le y\le 2; \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)=(x+y)^{2}.
$$

Now, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,y\le x\le 4-y,\,0\le y\le 2\},$ where $f(x,y)$ is nonzero.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14215461/assets/8d1935944ffa0017da736fc540ff823df8a052c2c32c985553cde08ea5fce8da.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{(X+Y)}^{2}] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}(x+y)^{2}\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}(x+y)^{2}\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y}^{4-y}(x+y)^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{3}(x+y)^{3}]}_{x=y}^{x=4-y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}[\frac{1}{3}(4-y+y)^{3}-\frac{1}{3}(y+y)^{3}]\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{12}{\int }_{0}^{2}({4}^{3}-(2y)^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{12}{\int }_{0}^{2}(64-8{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{12}{[64y-2{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(128-32) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find $\text{E}[{X}^{2}+{Y}^{2}],$ given that random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}xy,\, & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.
$$

Notice that $f(x,y)$ is nonzero only in the rectangular region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2\}.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}+{Y}^{2}] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{3}y+x{y}^{3})\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{y{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{3}{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{y}{4}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =[\frac{{y}^{2}}{8}+\frac{{y}^{4}}{8}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+2-0 \\  & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find $\text{E}[{X}^{3}(Y+1)],$ given that random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\, & 1\le x\le 3,\,1\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)={x}^{3}(y+1).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y)$ is nonzero only in the rectangular region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 3,\,1\le y\le 2\}.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{3}(Y+1)] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}{x}^{3}(y+1)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{3}(y+1)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{x}^{3}(y+1)\cdot \frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}y(y+1){\int }_{1}^{3}x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}y(y+1){[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}4y(y+1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{4{y}^{3}}{3}+2{y}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & ={[\frac{4{y}^{3}}{3}+2{y}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{32}{3}+8)-(\frac{4}{3}+2) \\  & =\frac{46}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find $\text{E}[{e}^{X-Y}],$ given that random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{y},\, & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)={e}^{x-y}.
$$

Notice that $f(x,y)$ is nonzero only in the rectangular region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡2\}.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{e}^{X-Y}] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}{e}^{x-y}\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}{e}^{x-y}\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x-y}\cdot {e}^{y}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}[{e}^{x}]_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(e-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =[(e-1)y]_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =(e-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$
